title: Al-Qabid, the Withholder
hookLine: the Withholder, who constricts as a test
tomorrow: after the tightening, does it ever open back up?

cards: A week can shrink. The to-do list grows, the money runs short, and the chest feels a size too small. Amira's has exams, Jordan home sick, and the inside wall still only half primed.

Yesterday's question: is a week like that a punishment? The Qur'an names that exact reaction. In Pickthall's words: "But whenever He trieth him by straitening his means of life, he saith: My Lord despiseth me."
And the next word is: Nay.

teach.b: Al-Qabid, the Withholder, who constricts, and in surah eighty-nine the tightening is called a trial, not a verdict. The Qur'an puts the pair in one breath: "Allah straiteneth and enlargeth."
So what exactly gets tightened? Two readings live inside the tradition.
View one: it's provision. Money, time, health, the means of life, narrowed for a season, as the verses about livelihood say. Their best case: it keeps the name honest and concrete.
A short paycheck isn't a metaphor, and the name speaks straight to it.
View two: it's also the heart.

Writers on the inner life, like al-Qushayri, describe qabd and bast, contraction and expansion, as states the heart passes through, sometimes with no outer reason at all: a heaviness on a day when nothing is wrong.
Their best case: some tight seasons have nothing to do with money, and the name reaches there too. The two views overlap more than they argue.
Both say the tightening comes from Him, both refuse to read it as hate, and both expect it to turn.
Here's something to tell a friend tonight: in the Qur'an's own words, the person who says my Lord despises me when things get tight hears back one word, nay.

how: In the traditional list of names al-Qabid stands beside al-Basit, the Expander, and the tradition treats hard seasons as trials to meet with patience and du'a.

o: the One who takes back gifts He regrets giving
the One who punishes the greedy with poverty
the One who tightens, for a season, as a trial

s: a tight season is a sign that Allah despises you
surah eighty-nine names that reaction and answers it: nay. the tightening is a trial.
some Muslim writers describe qabd as a state of the heart
al-Qushayri and others write of contraction and expansion of the heart.
the two views on al-Qabid disagree about whether it comes from Allah
both say it comes from Him and both refuse to read it as hate; they differ on what gets tightened.

games.q: your friend says al-Qabid is only about money and jobs. you lean toward 'it's the heart too.' to be fair, what's her best case?
o: the verses on al-Qabid speak of livelihood, and a short paycheck isn't a metaphor.
she doesn't like talking about feelings, so she keeps it to money.
the heart can't ever be tight unless money is short.
games.why: the provision reading stays close to the verses about livelihood. the heart reading, in writers like al-Qushayri, adds the tight days with no outer cause. both live inside the tradition.

practice: Close one hand into a loose fist and rest it on your knee. For the sit, let it stay closed, without squeezing harder and without forcing it open, and notice what a tight season feels like when nobody is fighting it.

wordCard.voice: Al-Qabid: the Withholder, who tightens provision or the heart for a season, as a trial and never as hate.

orig.note: Arabic: the Withholder, who constricts. beside al-Basit, the Expander, in the traditional list.

carryVoice: For the road: the tightening is a trial, not a verdict, and the Qur'an answers despair with nay. Until tomorrow.
